html:
A customs union of German states, led by Prussia, that came into force on 1 January 1834. Members dropped tariffs between themselves and set common tariffs at their outer borders.

After 1815 the German Confederation was a patchwork of dozens of states, each with its own tolls and duties, which choked trade. Prussia, itself split into an eastern and a western block, abolished its internal tolls in 1818 and drew its neighbours into a shared system. Most German states had joined by the 1850s. The economist Friedrich List argued for such a union and for German railways.

Austria stayed outside, which mattered. German trade and industry grew around Prussia, and the smaller states got used to its lead. Railways, coal and iron grew fast within the union.

The Zollverein knit the German economies together decades before political unity. When Otto von Bismarck united Germany under Prussia in 1871, after defeating Austria in 1866, much of the economic groundwork was already laid. Some historians caution that the union did not make unification certain, since some members sided with Austria in 1866.
